Together, With Ireland, Thailand will continue its work as informal co-facilitator on complementarity, helping to strengthen the links among these instruments. We also call for the early entry into force of the CTBT and urge the nuclear weapons states to sign and ratify the protocol to the Bangkok Treaty without reservations. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank you, Representative.

I thank Thailand, and I give the floor League of Arab States.

Thank you, President. Allow me to speak in Arabic.

Mr. President, as we commemorate this International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, we wish to take this opportunity to reiterate our commitment our commitment to one of the most pressing and long-standing commitments of the United Nations, that of definitively ridding humanity of these weapons which constitute an existential threat. We are very much concerned, in light of the exacerbation of geostrategic tensions and diminution of trust at the international level, the nuclear and the obstacles to the arms control regime. We know that nuclear weapons are being updated, and there's a new arms race, which is posing a threat with a deliberate or non-deliberate use of such weapons. We support the NPT and the balance between the three pillars. And in this regard, we deplore the failure of the review conference in 2026, its failure to adopt an outcome consensus-based document. This is the third consecutive time that this occurred. We call for the full integral fulfillment of all the commitments, beginning with disarmament commitments under Article VI. The mitigation -- threat mitigation measures under no circumstances should constitute an alternative to the complete elimination of nuclear weapons. We are following with great concern the incorporation of AI into command and controls and early warning systems. And in this respect, any decision to use this system as at all times must be under the control and full responsibility of human beings. The credibility of the nonproliferation regime can only be -- has not been fully achieved in the Middle East, and this is because Israel remains the only state in the region, non-state party to the NPT, which is not bringing its facilities under the IAEA safeguards oversight regime. For this reason, we once again call upon Israel to join the NPT as a non-nuclear-weapon state and to submit all of its facilities to the general safeguards. the comprehensive safeguards, we believe that the establishment of a nuclear -- a zone free of nuclear weapons and other WMDs in the Middle East remains an imperative at the international level. We applaud progress achieved during the International Conference on the Establishment of Said Zone, and we look forward to continuing this process during the seventh session under the chairmanship of the Sultanate of Oman. To conclude, the League of Arab States will spare no effort as we seek to achieve a nuclear-weapons-free zone and to guarantee security and equal footing for all states in the region. Thank you.
I thank the League of Arab States, and I now give the floor to the African Union.

Thank you, Mr. President. In the context of current geopolitics, the subject of the elimination of nuclear weapons is an increasingly relevant topic. and efforts to advocate for the prohibition of nuclear weapons are more relevant than ever. Current multidimensional tensions across the world are arguably testing the agility of the international community against nuclear warfare. Africa has long recognized the importance of denuclearization, beginning with the OAU's 1964 decision, later endorsed by the UN. The African Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty, Treaty of Pelindaba of 1996, in force since 2009, establishes Africa as a nuclear weapon free zone while permitting the peaceful use of nuclear science. The Pelindaba Treaty legally prohibits the research, development, stockpiling, testing, and stationing of nuclear explosive devices on African soil and its surrounding islands. The African Commission on Nuclear Energy plays an important role in bolstering compliance, maintaining safeguards, and fostering regional security cooperation. The continent speaks with moral clarity derived from rejecting weapons of mass destruction and prioritizing human security. We express deep concern over the dangerous slowdown in global disarmament and the massive financial reinvestments major nuclear powers are making in the modernization of their arsenals. Any use of nuclear weapons would trigger catastrophic and irreversible humanitarian and environmental devastation. We recall that the illegal exploitation of Africa's natural resources can contribute to nuclear catastrophe. Uranium from Africa under colonial rule contributed to the production of bombs used against Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Today, African Union member states with uranium and other critical minerals need to work in a united manner to ensure transparent and fair agreements that guarantee local benefits, environmental protection, skills development, and technology transfer, while ensuring Africa's resources serve peaceful development and not destructive purposes. While there was an absence of consensus on the outcomes of the 11th Review Conference held in May 2026, the Africa Group secured the retention of sovereign choices languages, which recalls on all States Parties to respect each country's decisions related to peaceful uses of nuclear energy, taking into account the needs of developing countries. Complementing these efforts, initiatives such as the African Union Fellowship on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation, launched in 2025 by the AU, equip regional stakeholders with the expertise and diplomatic skills needed to promote stability. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of the African Union, and I now give the floor to the Pan-African Intergovernmental Agency for Water and Sanitation for Africa.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, On behalf of the Permanent Observer Mission of Pan African Intergovernmental Agency for Water and Sanitation, I thank you for convening this meeting. Our mission works for one purpose, that every person has safe water and dignified sanitation. We speak today because nuclear weapons threaten that purpose more completely than almost anything else. Water has no borders. Radioactive contamination does not stop at a frontier, a river or an aquifer. Nuclear testing has already left lasting legacies in land and water, including the Algerian Sahara, where tests were carried out in the 1960s. Any use of nuclear weapons today will poison rivers, lakes, and groundwater for generations. It would destroy the water, power, and health systems that communities depend on, and it could disrupt rainfall and harvest far beyond the countries directly involved. No water or sanitation system in the world could withstand such catastrophe. Africa has made its choice. Through the Treaty, our continent is a nuclear-weapon-free zone. We urge all States to move with the same resolve towards the total elimination of nuclear weapons. Mr. President, our mission champions science-based solutions, and science points in two directions. First, science tells us the true cost of nuclear weapons. Research on nuclear testing and its effect on the environment and health must guide the policy. And communities affected by past testing must receive assistance and environmental remediation, including the restoration of safe water. Second, science can serve peace. The same nuclear science that built weapons of destruction can protect life. Isotope techniques help map and manage groundwater, trace pollutions, and plan for drought. Work the International Atomic Energy Agency support in many African countries. Every dollar spent on a nuclear arsenal is a dollar not spent on the pipes, wells, treatment, plants, and toilets that billions of people still lack. Mr. President, WASSA is not going to make suggestions, but rather remind us that water sustains life. Nuclear weapons threaten to end it. The choice before us is clear. Our mission and fund is support for the total elimination of nuclear weapons and for redirecting science, investment, and cooperation towards the needs of people and the planet. Let us build a world where water is shared as a source of peace. and never treated as a casualty of war. I thank you.
I thank you for your statement, and I now give the floor to the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies. I am honored to deliver this statement on behalf of the International Committee of the Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. In January 1946, less than six months after the horrific destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki by nuclear weapons and the loss of more than 140,000 lives, the UN General Assembly addressed nuclear disarmament as its very first action. Acting by consensus, the GA established a commission charged with making specific proposals for the elimination of atomic weapons from national armaments. 80 years later, the world seems to be walking backward and away from the goal of nuclear disarmament. Amid growing international and regional tensions, nuclear rhetoric has increased alarmingly, including explicit and implicit threats to use nuclear weapons. We are alarmed by both these developments and by the lack of urgent and focused collective response. Earlier this year, the 11th Review Conference of the NPT ended without agreement on a final document for a third consecutive time. Excellencies, the Japanese Red Cross was present when Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed, and it is today still responding to the effects. Our movement knows firsthand the horrific reality of nuclear weapons and the unacceptable human suffering they cause. Humanitarian consequences are what led the General Assembly to adopt its first resolution, and they are what drives the consistent call by the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement for the prohibition and elimination of nuclear weapons. The TPNW, which completes the international legal regime comprehensively prohibiting nuclear weapons, and weapons of mass destruction is now signed or ratified by 101 states. Its prohibition of nuclear weapons supports the cessation of the nuclear arms race and nuclear disarmament, thereby advancing implementation of Article VI of the NPT. We therefore reiterate our call on all states to adhere to the TPNW without further delay. Joining this treaty is a practical and effective step toward the ultimate goal of the NPT, namely to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons. Excellencies, in conclusion, we call on all states to pursue practical measures to reduce the risk of nuclear weapons being used. First, consistently and visibly highlight the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of any use of nuclear weapons. Second, condemn any threats to use nuclear weapons and any other rhetoric that erodes the taboo against their use. And third, ensure compliance with international humanitarian law at all times and undertake IHL compatibility assessments of current nuclear doctrines. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the International Committee for the Red Cross. We will now hear statements by civil society. I'd like to give the floor to the representative of Peace Boat.

Thank you, Mr. President, for this opportunity. Peace Boat has traveled with over 180 hibakusha, atomic bomb survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, sharing their testimonies worldwide. Through our global voyages, we also engage with survivors of nuclear testing, youth from affected islands, indigenous communities impacted by uranium mining, and nuclear disaster victims from all over the world known as global hibakusha. As an international steering group member of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, we call on all states to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons to ensure no one suffers as those survivors did. As part of the Japan Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, we urge Japan to not only maintain its three non-nuclear principles, but also to sign and ratify the TPNW as soon as possible. Listening to the testimonies of the hibakusha, who survived injuries, loss of loved ones, and the total destruction of their cities, and still suffer from medical and social and psychological impacts even 81 years later, makes clear that nuclear weapons are an issue of human rights and dignity. Today, nuclear weapons are developed in the name of national security and deployed under the theory of deterrence. In reality, what is threatened is our own right to live in peace. We welcome this month's first ever UN meeting on nuclear victims assistance and environmental remediation. As discussed, nuclear weapons use, testing, and production have brought immense suffering and environmental contamination worldwide. Such harm will continue as long as these weapons are developed and maintained, and we must stop this injustice now. We hope that discussions on concrete measures, including establishing an international trust fund and a gender-sensitive approach, will advance at the upcoming TPNW First Review Conference. The key is the participation of people impacted by nuclear weapons themselves in the design and implementation of such measures. Furthermore, we are alarmed at the buildup of nuclear arsenals by the nine nuclear-armed states, both in quantity and quality, and horrified at the increased risk of a nuclear war. We thus call on all states concerned to stop developing or deploying new nuclear weapons, including so-called tactical nuclear weapons, never resume nuclear test explosions, and to cease all nuclear testing, including subcritical tests, and stop missile tests and exercises for the delivery of nuclear weapons. We strongly reject the concept of usable tactical nuclear weapons. Such so-called low-yield weapons still have almost the same explosive power or even more than Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs. We must never repeat the catastrophe. Finally, we urge all UN member states to participate in the upcoming TPNW first review conference, reaffirm the unacceptable humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons, and declare a joint commitment to their total elimination. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Peace Boat. So we've come to the last statement of this high-level meeting of the General Assembly to celebrate and promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. I want to express my sincere gratitude to all the participants. for your contributions and ideas that you have shared with us at this high-level meeting. Consequently, we have concluded this high-level meeting. The meeting is adjourned.
